description.summary: Hybrid Retrieval combines candidate sets or scores from multiple retrieval approaches, commonly lexical and semantic retrieval, before context assembly.
description.description: Hybrid Retrieval retrieves candidates through multiple paths and combines their ranks, normalized scores, or candidate sets. Multiple paths do not guarantee a gain: effectiveness depends on complementarity, standalone path quality, query and document characteristics, fusion method and parameters, and candidate depth. A fused candidate set may be passed to a later reranker, but hybrid retrieval and reranking are distinct stages whose effects must be measured separately.
description.problemStatement: A single retrieval method can miss useful context when a query depends on exact terminology, semantic similarity, or both, while indiscriminately adding paths can introduce irrelevant candidates and operational cost.
description.coreIdea: Measure complementary retrievers independently, combine their candidate evidence with an explicit fusion policy, and retain only combinations whose evaluated benefit justifies their latency and resource overhead.
limitations: A weak or poorly matched path can degrade a fused result below the best constituent retriever.
Fusion effectiveness and operating cost can change with domain, query type, document structure, candidate depth, parameters, indexes, and deployment environment.
Retrieval-metric gains do not by themselves establish downstream RAG-generation gains.

evidence.summary: The SIGIR 2009 paper defines RRF with k=60 and reports that its pilot and TREC experiments beat Condorcet, CombMNZ, and the best system by 4 to 5 percent on average; its LETOR 3 meta-learner beat all individual rankings and Condorcet, while CombMNZ edged RRF non-significantly in that final experiment.
evidence.interpretation: RRF has strong historical evidence as a rank-fusion baseline, but its success should be tested again for each modern sparse-dense candidate set rather than presumed.

limitations: The evidence is limited to historical Wumpus pilot collections, TREC submitted-run fusion, and LETOR 3 learning-to-rank outputs.
TREC 9 included a human-in-the-loop best run that RRF did not beat; CombMNZ slightly exceeded RRF on LETOR 3 without a significant difference.
The experiments use MAP and do not evaluate current lexical-plus-embedding RAG pipelines, downstream generation, latency, storage, or indexing cost.
The reported significance tests do not establish universal improvement for every input ranking set.

evidence.summary: BGE M3-Embedding arXiv v1 Table 4 reports MLDR average nDCG@10 of 52.5 for Dense, 62.2 for Sparse, 64.8 for Dense+Sparse, and 65.0 when all three scores are summed; Dense+Sparse retrieves top-1000 candidates from each Dense and Sparse path and reranks their union by the sum of the two scores, while Multi-vec is optional later scoring rather than a third initial candidate path.
evidence.interpretation: Within BGE-M3, the sparse path supplied complementary long-document evidence beyond the dense path, while the incremental average gain from adding multi-vector scoring after Dense+Sparse was smaller.

inputRequirements.name: Retrievable corpus
inputRequirements.description: A corpus available through at least two retrieval signals or retriever configurations.

outputArtifacts.name: Merged retrieval candidates
outputArtifacts.description: A candidate set produced by combining results from complementary retrieval methods.

implementationConsiderations: Measure every constituent retriever independently on the target query distribution before fusion; exclude or down-weight paths that are consistently weak.
Choose rank-based fusion versus score-based fusion deliberately: rank fusion avoids cross-retriever score calibration, while score fusion requires scores to be normalized onto compatible scales.
Record the fusion method, smoothing constants, score-normalization procedure, path weights, and any query-dependent routing or weighting so results can be reproduced.
Deduplicate merged candidates with stable document identifiers and preserve deterministic tie handling.
Choose candidate depth independently for each retrieval path and choose the retained post-fusion depth separately; candidate depth affects both recall and noise.

Measure the slowest retrieval path as well as fusion overhead because parallel paths still delay completion until the required results arrive; also evaluate sequential execution when the deployment uses it.
Account for construction time, update cost, storage, memory, and operational ownership of every additional index rather than treating a second path as cost-free.
Preserve each candidate's per-path rank, raw score, normalized score, and inclusion reason so gains and weakest-link failures can be diagnosed.
Treat later cross-encoder, multi-vector, or other reranking as a separate stage with separate candidate-depth, effectiveness, latency, and cost measurements.
Do not assume one fusion method is universally optimal; compare rank-based and score-based alternatives under the target retrievers, domain, and constraints.
evaluationGuidance: Record each constituent retriever, model and index configuration, and its standalone Recall, MRR, nDCG, or other retrieval metrics before reporting a hybrid gain.
Record candidate depth per path, merged candidate-pool size, retained post-fusion depth, and the duplicate-handling policy.
Record the fusion method, all fusion parameters and weights, and score normalization or calibration used by score-based fusion.
Record dataset, domain, query length or query type, language, and document type and length so complementarity and weakest-link behavior can be segmented rather than hidden in an aggregate.
Use controlled ablations that compare each path alone, the same paths under alternative fusion methods, and the complete fused system to distinguish path addition from fusion effects.
When a later reranker is applied, report its input and retained depths and compare both pre-rerank and post-rerank results so hybrid candidate generation is not credited with the reranker's gain.

When downstream generation is evaluated, record the generator, prompt or generation configuration, number of context documents, and generation metric, and hold them constant across retrieval comparisons.

Measure end-to-end mean and P99 latency where available, throughput, index-construction time, index size, peak memory, hardware, batching, cache state, and whether paths execute in parallel or sequence.
Inspect per-path ranks and scores for failed queries to identify weak-path pollution, duplicate effects, score-calibration errors, and relevant documents omitted before fusion.
Report statistical tests or confidence intervals when available and explicitly disclose their absence for numerical comparisons.
